utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we have the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do have one item and let me begin with a bit of trepidation because I don't like to start a session with the understanding of the parties that perhaps I'm to cause disharmony in the court. We received the proofing notes from the Prosecution yesterday and I'm sure they were well intended in proofing this particular individual who has given a close to 90-page statement. But in the proofing notes, it appears from them, from the Prosecution, that they showed the gentleman certain documents in order to refresh his memory. Now, one of the documents that was shown to him appears to be a document that was generated and signed -- or we're a little unclear as to whether it was signed by Mr. Borovcanin. The unintended result may have been, in my opinion, that the individual's memory today and the testimony that we're about to hear is not from his memory, but rather from documents that may have been shown to him. And I am somewhat concerned of this practice. Again, I want to stress that I don't think that there was anything nefarious or sinister behind this, but I think there is an unintended result. The gentleman obviously was mixed up on a lot of things when he testified, or when he gave his statement. And I'm sure the effort was to try to at least give him an indication as to the dates, because he's off on various dates. However, I think the better practice would have been for this to have occurred in court, so at least we could first hear his independent memory, and then not necessarily be impeached but at that point he could be shown documents in order to aid him, arrive at a -- at the dates that he recollects when the certain events occurred. So the question is: What am I asking for? Well, at this point initially, and I must say that I was rather, shall I say, upset. That's a kind way of putting it when I saw this. Upon reflection, however, I've mellowed. And I would ask at the very minimum for the Court to keep -- to take this into consideration at the time of hearing his testimony. My initial reaction was to ask that this witness be disallowed from testifying because now we no longer have his independent memory but one that might have inadvertently been tampered with. When I say "tampered," I don't mean it in a bad sense but I'm saying it may have been, the word is escaping me, compromised. That's the more accurate phrase. And again I think it might have been -- I think it's an unintended result, but nonetheless -- so I think at a very minimum this Court should keep that in mind while hearing his testimony and factor that into its consideration when determining what weight, if any, to give to this gentleman's testimony. I would also like at some point, perhaps we could do this at a 65 ter meeting, but at some point come to some sort of ground rules with respect to proofing, because I do believe that this approach can be abused, and I'm not saying it was, but I'm saying it can be abused to the point where somebody could then come into court, testify from freshly -- a memory that is not independent, but rather one that was freshly created. So that's my point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any explanations or submissions from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't understand the concern here, frankly. For example, it's completely normal for a witness to be provided documents to help refresh his recollection. And I'll give you an example: Regarding the alleged Borovcanin document that we received well after this man's interview, which was a long time ago, as you know, it's unclear if that's an authentic document or not. And in that document, there is a statement on 12 July that talks about pioneers or deminers demining an area for Borovcanin's people as they go into Potocari. And as the Court knows and the Court gets copies of the proofing notes as well, of course, this witness -- and we should probably go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, I myself am not very familiar with this proofing session, because there was none of such kind of procedure in my jurisdictions. We only have a very strict rule in my jurisdiction that any rehearsal of the testimony is not allowed. But I understand that the proofing is not a rehearsal, it's just to refresh the memory of the witnesses and to try to avoid any unnecessary direct examination or cross-examination in this aspect. So I believe that Mr. Karnavas raises a very good issue. It's about the proofing process in this Tribunal. I hope during the winter recess, the parties will have some homework, to do some research on this aspect, and after the recess we could get the submissions from the parties concerning of this proofing process. As for this particular witness, of course we are going to hear this witness while bearing in mind the submissions by the parties, both Mr. Karnavas and Mr. McCloskey. Well, having said that, could we have the witness, please. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It might be good to go into private session just briefly for the witness information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean when we have the witness or before the witness? When we have the witness? Well, it seems to me that according to our calendar, this week we only have three sittings. It is our intention that we would like to finish the testimony of this witness within this week. Actually, three days is just only eight sittings. Normally we do not limit the time on the direct or cross-examination, but since this week we'll two days on the plenary meetings of the Judges as well as a sentencing hearing of another case. So, Mr. McCloskey, could you please indicate how much time you need for the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I hope only two sessions, though we'll see how the witness does in his memory and things. But hopefully two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I can -- I've looked at the indictment, and this gentleman is almost in the entire indictment, on every count, mentioned. He's given, as I've indicated, close to an 80-page or 90-page statement. I think it's 86, to be exact. And then in light of some new, or slightly different information that we're getting from the proofing notes and in light of the way the statement went when it was taken, and I think Mr. McCloskey will agree with me that it was somewhat confusing. I will need two days. This is an important witness. I intend to be extremely efficient, but there is a lot of material to cover, Your Honour. This is -- and as you've seen me on several occasions just last week, I didn't even ask a question. So, I think that you know that I only ask questions when it's necessary. They may not be the right questions, but at least -- so I will try to be as efficient as possible. I think I can handle it within four to five sessions, but I truly -- and it all depends on how responsive the gentleman is. It may turn out that he's very responsive and I could do it in less, but he is a critical witness, Your Honour. And I say this with all due sincerity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. When we were preparing for the cross-examination of this witness, we thought maybe we wouldn't cross-examine him on anything else but the general circumstances and their joint work after the war. Since we received this proofing earlier this morning in which he mentioned Jokic in relation to the events after that took place in Srebrenica, we believe that we will have some question and that it will take some half an hour to 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Karnavas, I hope you could do your cross-examination in four or five sessions, otherwise we have to keep this witness over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It will be done, Your Honour. It will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may sit down, please. And shall we go to private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can have him do this first so we have this for the record, Your Honour, and he knows and just private session for just a moment. Examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could just take a look at that piece of paper. Don't read it out, but can you tell us, is that your name on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session just briefly for some background questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how long were you in that school in Rajlovac near Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: In 1992, I moved to Sombor to continue my education there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you continue your education there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: For another year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I returned to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what year was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you return in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Because I failed to pass my exams in the secondary military school, and I wanted to return to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you returned to Bosnia, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I continued my education in the secondary school in Bratunac, and I completed the third year of the secondary school for electrical technicians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Then I applied for the -- for a place at the academy in Banja Luka to join the engineers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that a civilian or military organisation you wanted to join?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this -- in the engineers, was it a civilian engineering or was it a military engineering organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you become a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get to this academy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you start taking classes at this academy, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I believe that it was in June 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you study at this academy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: For almost a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any -- were you given any combat experience during that time that you were taking classes in Banja Luka at the academy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Are you asking me about my initial combat experience or my combat experience in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us -- outline your combat experience that you were able to get while you were at school in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: On two occasions, I went to the frontline. The first time I went to Bihac and the second time I went to Grahovo, but I'm not sure. In any case, I was sent to the frontline twice while I was at school in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you receiving training in in that school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: To become a member of engineers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get any practical engineering-type experience in your combat tours that you just spoke of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, what kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I learned about mines, the anti-personnel mines and the anti-tank mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of your schooling period, where were you sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I was sent to the corps, which was in Vlasenica, and after that, I assigned to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private just for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is there a particular event that you recall seeing related to the capture of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the Serbian flag being hoisted on the Serbian church in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you actually see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you remembered being -- hearing about the flag or seeing the flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: At Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember if anyone was with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I remember that there were perhaps about ten people with me, and I think they included Colonel Blagojevic. If you are referring to that. Is that your question, whether Colonel Blagojevic was with me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That day the flag went up on the Serbian church in Srebrenica. Is that what you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that Colonel Blagojevic was with us then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember roughly about what time of day it was when the flag came up over the church?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: It's very hard to remember the time, but I think it was about 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to the day before that -- well, sorry. First of all, do you remember the date that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I think it was the 11th, June or July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then let me ask you: On the morning of the 10th, the day before the flag first came up on the church, do you remember where you woke up on the morning of the 10th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. I woke up in the headquarters of the 3rd Company in Pribicevac -- I'm sorry. I have to mention that I have a problem with remembering dates, and the entire statement I gave -- I mean, all the facts I gave are true facts, but I cannot be sure about the dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's why I want to make sure we're talking about now the day before Srebrenica fell. Okay. So, again, where were you -- where did you wake up the day before Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: At the headquarters of the 3rd Battalion at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: What I did when I woke up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you -- just outline what you did that morning, who you saw, any orders you received, what you did. Just outline us your day, if you could.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I was awakened by a strong explosion. I woke up. I wasn't sure who all the people at the headquarters were. A messenger came and told me that General Krstic was at the observation post and Colonel Blagojevic, too, and that they were looking for me. I came to the observation point. General Krstic explained to me that on the road to Slapovici from Zeleni Jadar, there was some kind of a fortification obstacle, that they cannot cross over with their technical equipment, so the ULT machine had to be taken down and the road had to be cleared for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did he give you any orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: To go with the machine down there, to find the operator of that machine, and to help that unit surmount that fortification obstacle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where Mr. Blagojevic was when General Krstic gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I think he was at the observation point with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, was he within earshot to have heard the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do when General Krstic gave you this order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I called Colonel Blagojevic. I asked him what to do in this respect, because I did not have this machine and I did not know how to operate the machine and I did not have any fuel either. So I asked him what to do with regard to this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask this of Mr. Blagojevic in the presence of General Krstic or out of General Krstic's presence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I called Colonel Blagojevic; I think that General Krstic didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how soon after receiving the order from General Krstic did you call Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did Colonel Blagojevic say to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I tried to explain the situation to him, that speaking quite realistically I cannot carry out that task. He told me to try to make an effort, that it was very important for me to complete that task. Perhaps those were not his exact words, but that was the context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went back to the command from the observation point. I found the operator of the machine. I found the operator in charge of fuel. I fueled up, and I took my men and went with the machine to Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many men did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether all the people from that platoon were with me. Perhaps five or six men. I'm not sure. I'm not sure about the figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who the ULT belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I think it belonged to the engineering regiment from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And tell us what you did with your men and this ULT that morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went to Zeleni Jadar and reported to the commander of the unit who was there, down there. I consulted him as to whether it was safe for me to do what I was supposed to do, because according to the explanation of this assignment, I was supposed to go in front of the frontline with the machine. I asked the commander of this unit whether it was safe to do that, and his explanation was that it was safe. When we set out to eliminate this material that was on the road, some weapons started shooting at the machine. The machine was not an armoured machine and it had no protection. In terms of such tasks or work, if I can put it that way, we had to go back. We couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was this commander of the unit down there at Zeleni that you were talking to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: People said that this was Legenda. I don't know him personally and I don't know whether that was him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do after that, after they started shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: We went back to the frontline that was held by our side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what orders did you get then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went back to Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever -- were you ever able to get rid of that obstruction with the ULT?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the operator returned after that to eliminate this material or whether the tanks and the Pragas went around the obstacle. At any rate, I didn't manage to get rid of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling us yesterday in my office something about this obstacle being -- gotten rid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I think so, yes, because they did manage to reach the village of Slapovici with all this technical equipment, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did anything happen on the way back to Pribicevac with you and your men and the ULT?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did on the way back and what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: One of my soldiers used the ULT to take a refrigerator and a TV set, put it in the bucket of the ULT. As we were driving towards Pribicevac, a jeep appeared, a PUH jeep, and General Mladic got out of it, as well as a few policemen. One had a camera. He started shouting at us. While others are waging war, you are stealing. A man from the security slapped one of my soldiers, and I was given the order to take the machine back to Pribicevac, together with the operator, and that the other soldiers were supposed to run in front of the PUH jeep all the way to Srebrenica. I beg your pardon. And also that we had to unload everything that was in the bucket and to leave it on the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did your soldiers have to run in front of Mladic's jeep towards Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I don't think so. Srebrenica hadn't been freed yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I mean did they have to run in front of the jeep from where you were towards -- down towards Zeleni Jadar area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. I think they ran to the first curve ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then what did you do the rest of that day, this day being the day before Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went back to Pribicevac. I reported to Colonel Blagojevic. I'm not sure whether I found Colonel Blagojevic or whether I reported to the commander of the 3rd Battalion, saying that I did not manage to carry out the task. Again, I'm saying I'm not sure whether it happened on that particular day, but I think that I did report to the commander of the 3rd Battalion. And that then via radio communications, I heard that Cvijetin Petrovic had been wounded, that they were asking for an ambulance to come and fetch him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you remember if you did any other work that day, the day before Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Well, I opened the road leading to the minefield near Pribicevac, so that the 4th Company could have access in view of the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, getting to the day Srebrenica fell, what did you do that day before you were at Pribicevac with others in the afternoon, evening, when the flag was raised above the church? Do you remember what you did the morning and the afternoon of the day Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think -- I'm really not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How about after the flag was raised. In the evening, early evening hours of 11 July, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I was at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go anywhere from Pribicevac that day, the day Srebrenica fell, that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It is possible that I went to the 2nd Battalion to get a man there who would open the minefield for the unit that was supposed to pass that way. I'm not sure. I think it is Lovanacki Potok [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day Srebrenica fell, did you go into Srebrenica at all to do any work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive orders to go into Srebrenica to do work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I don't know whether it can be called an order. A day before Srebrenica fell, I was standing at Pribicevac with Colonel Blagojevic when a truck came with a launcher. And they tried to launch a rocket at one of the hills where the enemy was. This rocket was not fired. It stayed right there in front of the truck. I think that on that day when talking to Colonel Blagojevic -- I mean, I cannot call it an order, but as I spoke with him, I came to the conclusion myself -- I mean, during this conversation with Colonel Blagojevic. Actually, we concluded together that the enemy would try, if our units would enter Srebrenica, to leave booby traps all over. I was supposed to follow our units with my team and to try to deactivate as many mines as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So on the day Srebrenica fell and the VRS was able to go into Srebrenica, why did you yourself go into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: To take care of booby traps, to eliminate them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that based on the -- your conversation you had the previous day with Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. And it was only natural -- it was only to be expected that I should go to Srebrenica too, because actually everybody was there, all the units. No one was left at Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone order people to go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Well, I think that in the afternoon, General Mladic appeared and said that everybody had to go ahead, that our units were advancing. I did not hear this, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Somebody told you about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Not me, not me. Everybody was talking about it, that the general had been there and that he made everybody leave Pribicevac and go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night that afternoon/evening that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I stayed at one of the Muslim houses with my team of young men. We spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the next morning, the day after Srebrenica fell, what did you and your men do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: We were working on demining booby traps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how late that day did you work? When did you stop work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Until late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what did you do when you stopped work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: We went to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Because I didn't have enough equipment left anymore for removing the booby traps. I did not have fuel for my vehicle. I needed logistical support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How -- which route did you take back to Bratunac, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: We could not go through Potocari. We went along the Srebrenica/Oljavica road. Perhaps it's not that road. We went back with a strange vehicle. We managed to get into that vehicle and take that vehicle, because we did not have fuel for our truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose vehicle was that that you got into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it was a UN Amphibia vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what colour it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I think it was white.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time did you get back, roughly, to Bratunac on that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: It was around -- maybe, I'm in the sure, but it was sometime between 3.00 and 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when was the next time that you went on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went home. I took a bath. I had something to eat, and then I went back to the command around -- I don't know about the time, but it was before 8.00 in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the second day after Srebrenica fell. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. We are now talking about the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if Srebrenica fell on the 11th and you spent the night at a Muslim house on the night of the 11th, like you've described, and you worked all day in Srebrenica on the 12th, then you went to Bratunac late night and arrived home 3.00 a.m. the 13th. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I must repeat that I have a problem with dates and times. It was eight and a half years ago, a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were about 19 years old at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- so when you got to the brigade command at 8.00 a.m., what -- did you receive any instructions from anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I tried to get in touch with Colonel Blagojevic; however, I am not sure but I believe that I couldn't get in touch with him. I didn't speak to him. I received an order to escort and monitor -- to monitor possible groups of enemies and to try and find the record of the minefield on the lines that used to be held by the enemy. I'm not sure who gave me that order, whether it was Colonel Blagojevic, Lieutenant Colonel Pajic, or some other officer from the command. Very often it would happen that my senior colleagues could also give me orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did anyone that morning of the 13th tell you to go to Srebrenica to do more booby trapping, before you got this order to look for mine information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I believe that I found Lieutenant Colonel Pajic. I really can't remember, but I believe that I reported to Lieutenant Colonel Pajic and I told him I didn't have enough equipment and enough men to go there, that there were too many civilians in the town, that I can't remove booby traps just like that, that it was not easy to do, that I needed fuel, that I needed protective gear and things like that. But I'm not sure. I can't claim that Lieutenant Colonel Pajic ordered me to go and search for the record of the minefields. It is quite possible -- there is a strong possibility that I myself concluded that this is something that should be done. I can't say for a fact that I was given such an order or -- but I'm sure that I gave a report to somebody that I couldn't do something like that in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you go to Srebrenica that day, the 13th, at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: It is possible. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did a senior officer give you instructions or an order to get the mine information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm saying I'm not sure. There is a possibility that I was told that my Lieutenant Colonel Pajic, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what did you do that day, on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I was in the command. I'm not sure about the time, but in the streets, in the town, I saw buses parked in the streets. There were people sitting on those buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: They were detainees from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any women on those buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what did you do? What did you do that day that you saw these buses with detainees in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: First I went to the primary school, Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you decide to go to a school that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Because all of the buses -- there was a column of buses, and they were all on the way to the school, that is, from the bus station, the road went to the left, and all the buses that were parked were on that street that led to the school. It is possible that I may have inquired and asked people around whether there were any other detainees anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your purpose of going to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went there to try and find somebody who could give me instructions about where I could find a record of the minefields on the frontline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What school did you first go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: First I went to the Vuk Stefanovic Karadzic school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any soldiers guarding that school when you got to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: The military police were in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what unit -- what brigade were those military police from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: They had the Bratunac Brigade insignia and white military police belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you recognise anyone that you knew from the Bratunac Brigade military police around that school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I recognised the Pinzgauer operator and that Pinzgauer was parked in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that Pinzgauer operator that you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I knew the man's nickname Trocijevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what unit was he from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure but I believe he was from the sabotage platoon of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Pinzgauer, can you describe this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: It's a classical military vehicle with an open top and a firm metal cap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything mounted on it, any weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: There was a machine gun, 12.7-millimetre Browning machine gun mounted on top of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that machine gun have anything to do with the nickname of your friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I believe so, although that particular piece does not have three barrels as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His nickname has something to do with three barrels I guess then. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see anybody you recognised in particular from the Bratunac Brigade military police that evening around this Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I saw the commander of the military police. I believe that his name was Mirko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it have been Mirko Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. I'm not sure. Either Jankovic or Stojanovic. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you first see the commander of the Bratunac Brigade military police, this Mirko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: The first time I saw him at the entrance to the primary school. He was trying to make three military policemen to get up to the second floor of the primary school, where nobody wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see, and what happened? What did he say to these guys? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: He asked them to go up there; however, they refused to carry out the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Nothing. These guys just didn't go up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly how many military police from Bratunac you saw in and around the school that evening.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure, maybe 10, 15, maybe less or maybe more. I don't know. I didn't count heads. This was not my goal. My goal was to try and establish a contact with the detainees in order to locate a record of the minefields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to get into the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell anyone under whose authority you were working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. I told a soldier at the entrance that Colonel Blagojevic had ordered me to get in and try and locate a record of the minefields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember today if that was true or you were just saying it so you could get in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: That is precisely why I said it. It made it simpler to get in the school. Having heard Colonel Blagojevic's name, the soldier didn't ask me any questions. So it made the whole thing much simpler for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you seen any Muslims on the outside of the school before you went into it at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: On the right-hand side I saw a leg, not a whole body, a leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was there -- do you think there was a whole body attached to that leg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is that a smirk on your face? Are you laughing?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm just try to find out. Because it sounds like you just see a leg lying there, and we know that -- I know that's not true, so I'm just try to clarify whether or not there's -- you can describe what is there. I'm sorry, I don't mean to be smiling. I shouldn't. I --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I explained to the soldier why I was there. And from that man I heard a person screaming. I asked the soldier what had happened to this man, and then the soldier told me that this man was up at the window, that he was cursing their Chetnik mothers, that he was provoking them all the time, and that finally he jumped from that window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: That may have been the truth, but it didn't have to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break at -- we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us how many floors the Vuk Karadzic school had.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, I didn't -- there was some distortion. I didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And were you able to go into the school this first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: To the second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, because some places the floors are counted differently. So when you say "the second floor," is there a ground floor and then a first floor and then a second floor above it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: The school did have a ground floor, a first floor, and a second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell from your visit to that school how full it was of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: On the ground floor, there were not that many people. It was not full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: What I could see were people in the hallways sitting down with their hands on their heads. And they were some 2 and a half to 3 metres from the stairway. I didn't enter any other rooms; I just entered the hallway. 2 and a half to 3 metres were left empty for people to go up to higher floors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second floor, were there any people on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How full from what you could see was the second floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: The hallway was full of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I believe that they were the former soldiers of the Srebrenica army, but they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any women at the school, any Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time when you're at the school, did you see any injured Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: One Muslim was injured, and I saw him on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of injury? Could you tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. It was dark. I couldn't see too well. He was asking for water. That's what I heard; he was asking for water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do when you went into the school? What did you try to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I tried to make contact. I tried to establish a contact with the detainees in order to carry out my mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, just what was the mission then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: To try and find somebody who would be able to tell me something about the mined fields which had been left behind by the Muslims where their defence lines used to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any success that time at the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: What kind of success do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Success in terms of finding mine information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No, I wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do after going to the Vuk Karadzic school? Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Well, I was talking about the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Where did you go after you went into the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I got in touch with a colleague of mine. He told me that he had saw -- seen a person called Sejo, and that person was on the second floor. He also told me that he knew him personally, and that person, I concluded, would be my best chance at a contact with somebody. I asked him whether Sejo could be found in one of the rooms or in the hallway, and I received information from an elderly person. And I concluded that he wasn't Sejo judging by his voice. The person who called me, who answered me, may have been about 50 years of age. I told him that he was not the Sejo that I was looking for, that the Sejo that I was looking for was a younger man, somebody who was about 23 to 27 years of age. And then this Sejo called out to me after that. I asked him to step out. I was standing on the top of the stairway on the second floor, some 2 and a half to 3 metres from the people who were sitting down there in the hall. At the beginning he didn't want to walk up to me. He was afraid. He asked me who I was. Finally he did come up to me. He asked for a cigarette. I had five or six cigarettes; I gave him those cigarettes. He was not able to talk to me in a normal fashion, so I could not expect any kind of assistance from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean he was not able to talk to you in a normal fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Maybe he was afraid or maybe he simply didn't want to talk to me, because he didn't know him -- know me personally and vice versa, I didn't know him either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the person who had given you information to contact Sejo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: That was Goran -- I can't remember his last name. His nickname was Bundeva. He was a mate of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what -- was he in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. He was not a member of the Bratunac Brigade. He was too young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was he then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was it that he had information about someone that might have mine information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this Goran the person that had told you to find Pejo [sic], that Pejo [sic] might have mine information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. He didn't tell me that. He only told me that he had seen Sejo in the school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Where were you talking to Goran when you learned this information that Goran gave you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: On the way to the school, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you go to any other buildings around the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go next after the Vuk Karadzic school? What was the next building you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: There was a building called the hangar. That was a building that was used for the training of car mechanics from the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that in relation to the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: On the back, viewed from the street. Perhaps 150 to -- perhaps 50 to 100 metres away from the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you marked that on an aerial photograph for us during your first interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go over that at the end, I think. Okay. And how did you get into the hangar? Did you have to talk to anyone before going in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: On the hangar door, there were two civilian policemen standing beside the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you say to them when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I said that I was trying to find the Sappers. I explained that I needed to find a Sapper, a man, who could give me information about minefields across the enemy line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you find when you went into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I saw people inside in this building; they were not sitting. I saw that some of them were smoking. Perhaps the atmosphere was a bit more relaxed than at the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the hangar? Was it broken up into different rooms? Is it one big open area? How is that? Can you just describe it briefly for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: There were three or four separate classrooms, and there was a big hangar. And that is where vehicles were repaired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it that you saw people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: They were not in the halls. The halls were empty -- the hall was empty. People were standing around in the classrooms, and a number of people were at the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just say roughly how many people you saw in the hangar that night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More than ten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More than 100?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the hangar have more than one ground floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand this. I didn't understand the interpretation I got. Ground level?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many levels did the hangar have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Thank you. One, one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So there was no stairs leading up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about what you saw when you saw these people in the hangar that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I think that at the entrance into the hangar, on the side in the hall, I saw blood on the left-hand side, on the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these Muslim men in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the Muslim men in the hangar were injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any information about mines from any of the men in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Well, I managed. In one of the classrooms I handed out a pack of cigarettes and I tried to talk to people; however, the information was unimportant. It was not information that I could use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how long did you stay in the hangar that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Perhaps five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how long had you spent in the Vuk Karadzic school before going to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Perhaps -- well, I'm not sure. Half an hour maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you go after the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went to the school. The name of the school is Slobodo, ime ti je Tito; Freedom, your name is Tito.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how close is that to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: About 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And like you have before, can you tell us what happened at the school. Did you -- were you allowed in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. I could come in. I explained to the people at the door what my mission was. I got in. I tried to talk to people. Of course, again nobody wanted to talk to me. Everybody just looked at me and nobody gave me any information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at this third school, do you know what sorts of people were guarding it outside, where they were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the people that were guarding it were wearing, what kind of clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No, no, I'd have to guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this third school, did you see any Serbs on duty inside the school, when you went inside the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I think that -- no, no. I didn't find anyone before I got in. Yes, I remember now. I remember now. There was a civilian policeman and there was a military policeman. The military policeman showed me in and he took me through all these room where these people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what unit this military policeman was from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think he was from the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think he was from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Because he had a uniform that was similar to mine. I'm not sure, but I think he had a uniform that was similar to my own. When I say "uniform," I'm referring to the colour, the same colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had described the Bratunac Brigade military police patch when you saw people outside the Vuk Karadzic school. Did you see this guy in this other school with any patches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I don't remember. I saw white belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I forgot to ask you about the hangar. Let me ask you -- sorry to take you back, but did you see any Serbs inside the hangar where the Muslim men were, like guarding them or doing anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. There was no one inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and the third school near the hangar, how many levels did it have, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Sorry, two. Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, were there prisoners on both levels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. I think that the prisoners were only at the lower level in three rooms, in three former classrooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the atmosphere in these three classrooms, how crowded it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: The atmosphere was -- well, when the door would open, people were afraid and they would look at us. That is how crowded they were. Not as much as in the first school, though. People were not sitting on the floor; they were walking around, smoking. And nobody wanted to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly what time of day it is that you were going to these three schools that are close to each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: It might have been -- well, I'm not sure. Maybe in the afternoon -- I don't know. I'm not sure. I would just have to guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get any information at the third school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. No one wanted to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That is a confusing question. I should say the school after the hangar, that's actually the second school. I take it your answer is the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you get any rough idea how many prisoners were in this third building that you had gone into that afternoon, evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: It is very hard for me to make any guesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see anybody injured in this third building at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these also Muslim men in this third building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so what did you do after this third building? Can you tell me -- I'm sorry, roughly how long did you spend at this third building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: After that, I went back to the Vuk Karadzic school, in front of the Vuk Karadzic school, where I had left my vehicle. I saw that it was too risky for me to try to talk to people on the bus, because I had seen three or four incidents of people breaking windows, swearing. I didn't think it was safe enough for me to try to talk to these people. Maybe my presence would cause more problems, because I had already seen that people were not willing to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People that were breaking windows, were those Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the bus or buses that you saw them in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: They were parked in the street, facing the centre of the town if you look at it from the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How near the front of the Vuk Karadzic school were the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Perhaps about 100 metres, 200 metres from the entrance into the building -- no, not 200. 100 metres at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I walked around the entire line of vehicles. There were some people in the field. This column of buses included two or three buses in the street, towards the monument of that same school. I went that way. I got to the monument. I think there were two more buses there. I realised then that there was no point in trying to talk to these people, that I could only upset them. I got into the car and set out towards Konjevic Polje. I thought that most people had set out towards Tuzla, and that our forces would probably have the largest number of prisoners in Konjevic Polje, because -- well, that is what I thought at the time. It was logical to expect that most people who did not want to be taken prisoner would set out for Tuzla. I came across our people in uniform along the way. I asked them whether they saw a group of people anywhere who had been taken prisoner so that I'd get any kind of information. However, I got my first answer somewhere in the village of Kajici. A soldier in uniform, I think he could have been from the Workers' Battalion. He was wearing camouflage trousers and a blue workers' jacket. He was a man of 50 or 55 perhaps. I put the same question to him as I had to everyone else previously. He told me that he saw that there were prisoners at the school in Kravica. I set out to Kravica, to the school there. I came to the parking area in front of the school. A man was standing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you just a question or two. The person that you thought was in the Workers' Battalion, what do you mean by the Workers' Battalion? What unit is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: That was a unit that had work obligation. They were not at the front line. They were mobilised when necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this man armed that gave you the information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He had some kind of a rifle on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other armed people nearby him or with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. He was alone and he seemed disoriented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise him being from anywhere, his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why do you think he was from the Workers' Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: These people usually had those blue jackets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you got to the front of the school in Kravica, tell us about that and what you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I walked up to him. I knelt by him. I asked him: What happened to you? He said that he had been hit, that he felt very bad, that he needed water. I asked him -- I mean, I said that in that condition he shouldn't drink any water. He said to me -- or rather, he was in very poor shape. He couldn't say much, but he just kept saying: "Water, water," to me. Finally I did bring him some water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How bad was his wound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but he looked pretty bad to me, his face did. I didn't summon the courage to ask him. I don't know. I don't know. It had a different effect on me when I saw a man whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling us that you could see his insides coming out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No, not that much, but I did see that he had a wound, a very big one on the left-hand side. I'm not sure that I saw his insides, but he looked pretty bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back to the person in a uniform you didn't recognise, do you know, have any idea, if that was a civilian or a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: It was a uniform that I had not seen until then. There was a pattern on the uniform that we had not used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the background colour, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Purple, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody that appeared to be in Bratunac Brigade uniforms around the Kravica school or inside it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anyone, and I found that very strange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling Mr. Manning that the person guarding the Kravica school was in a Bratunac Brigade uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No. No. I don't remember that. It was a uniform that was very different, but it would happen that people would find uniforms elsewhere, believing that they were better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, were there any Serbs inside this school with the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly how many Muslim prisoners you saw in this school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'd have to guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. More than ten? I don't want you to guess, but was it more than ten as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were more than ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate? I don't want you to guess, but just -- can you give us some feeling.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Do I have to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You don't have to guess and you don't have to speculate. So if you're not sure, you just tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but there were more than ten people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see anyone, while you were there, ever treating your friend that had this serious wound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at the Kravica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Maybe 15 minutes, and out of those 15 it took me 5 minutes to get water for my mate. There is a well right in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any information about minefields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I asked people again whether anybody knew anything about the person or the place where I could find records of the minefields, and nobody said anything to me -- I apologise. Muhamed told me that -- I can't quote him, but I believe that the point was that that person had left for Tuzla, the person who was responsible for setting the mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so where did you go after the Kravica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I returned to Bratunac. I believe that it was pointless for me to stay there, so I set out for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any big buses or trucks in Kravica town or around the road by Kravica or in front of the Kravica supermarket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: At the entrance to the town, I heard and I saw a vehicle of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, and I saw Mirko, the commander, who was calling people to help him and help the people who - I don't know how to explain that - who were providing security. He explained that there were 30 or 40 of us, that there were too many detainees, and that we were not able to control all of them, there was too few of us. Having heard that information, I reported to the school and I went up to the second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point that evening, did you go back to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go back to the Bratunac Brigade after you left the schools and report the findings of your research into mine information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: My plan was to return from Konjevic Polje and to report to the duty operations officer or Lieutenant Colonel Pajic and tell them whether I was successful or not. However, at the entrance to the town, I heard Mirko and I thought that that was more important. I went to the school and I went up to the second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling Dean Manning that after the schools you went back to the brigade headquarters and called on the internal phone, which you called the induction phone, and that you spoke to your commander, Blagojevic, and told him that you had not been able to find any mine information? Do you remember telling Mr. Manning that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it is possible that I told him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall telling me and Mr. Bruce Bursik the same identical information yesterday in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure. At the beginning of my conversation with you, I tried to explain to you that my recollection of these dates is rather bad and that it was possible and that you should give me time to think. But now at this moment, I would like to state that I thought it was more important for me to go to the school and help the people there, because in any case I -- my mission had not been successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you withdrawing the statement you made to Mr. Bursik yesterday, that you had reported to Blagojevic, or are you just mixed up about when you did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm still confused. I'm not sure. It -- maybe I did go to the command, but I'm not sure. It is possible that I went to the command and reported on what I had done before I went to the school. That would be the usual procedure, that is, reporting after a mission whether the mission was successful or unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've got a copy of the transcript, and if you could go to page -- excuse me. In the English, it's page 39, line 14 -- excuse me, it's page 65, line 17. In your page it's page 39, line 14. Tell me if you remember this. Dean Manning: "So it's 1425 hours. We've resumed the record conversation. You were telling me that you left the Kravica village and you went back to Bratunac. When you got back to Bratunac, what did you do? Did you go and report what you found?" Your answer was: "Yes." And Dean Manning said: "Think very carefully. You come back to Bratunac, who do you report to?" And you say: "I went to the brigade command and Colonel Blagojevic was there. I think he was in a meeting, and I spoke to him on the phone and I told him that I did not find any lists." Dean Manning says: "What meeting was he in?" You say: "He may have had a visitor. I was not present in any of those meetings because I was so young, and anyway, all the duties had to do with the chief of engineers. They were carried out by Colonel Blagojevic because he was an engineer." And then Dean Manning says: "I think so." Then you say: "I was just his hand in the field as far as the engineers matter." Then Dean Manning says: "Did you make the telephone call internally through the brigade, or were you in his reception area? Were you part of the brigade commander's office?" And you say: "It was the telephone 63, so-called induction connection, induction phone, that's what it's called. That line." Do you recall giving that answer to Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a true statement of what you told Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Would you give me a second to think?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You should also go on and look at page 39, line 47. And you go on to say: "I told him I did not find any of the miners, engineers. I did not have much time to talk to him, so it was a very short, a very brief conversation. I wasn't any kind of long story. I just told him, I did not find any of the lists from their miners." And Mr. Manning asked you what happened after that. And a few lines down you say: "Nothing. He just said 'okay,' and that was that." Were you -- was this the truth when you told it to Mr. Manning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: When I spoke to Mr. Manning in Banja Luka, in the UN head base there, there's probably a reason why I told him this. I can't remember this reason at this moment. I'm not sure that I found Colonel Blagojevic on that day in the brigade. I cannot confirm the information that I found Colonel Blagojevic upon my arrival from Kravica in the brigade command. I cannot do that. I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what do you remember after coming back from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I may have gone to the brigade command, but had I spoken to Colonel Blagojevic, I would remember that. I would be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I went to the Vuk Karadzic school, to the second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you think we made up those words that I read to you about the conversation with Dean Manning, where you report on the induction phone to Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Do I have to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a problem with the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I don't want to say that anybody is lying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking: Did you say that to Dean Manning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: I've just explained to you that when I said this, that there was a reason for me to say it. This was three and a half years ago. I can't remember the reason now, and that is why I cannot confirm that I spoke to Colonel Blagojevic upon my return from Kravica. And that is all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did, in fact, say that, what I had read, to Dean Manning; you just can't remember why you said it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So where did you go after the Kravica school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-135
